categories.name: Fabric notes
categories.description: Cloth, mills and how things wear.

posts.title: Dressing for the 7:40 tram
posts.excerpt: What we wear on a damp commute, and why the shirt matters more than the coat.
posts.content:
Our test commute starts at a tram stop on SE Division. The 7:40 is usually full, the seats are often damp, and by the time you arrive at your desk the shirt has been squeezed, leaned on and rained on. It is the best place we know to find out whether clothes are really everyday clothes.

A good commuting shirt does three things. It does not show creases, so a washed cotton oxford beats a crisp poplin. It breathes, so the collar is soft and the cuffs open. And it looks fine untucked, because nobody has time to tuck on a tram.

Our Easy Oxford Shirt came out of this test. It has a longer back hem, a collar that lies flat without a stay, and a fabric that gets better as it is washed. We wear ours with a chino or the wide trouser and a merino cardigan on top.

posts.title: The loopback sweatshirt, two winters in
posts.excerpt: A long-term note on a heavy cotton sweatshirt and what two winters did to it.
posts.content:
Loopback is the knit used on the inside of a classic sweatshirt: tiny loops of yarn that trap warm air. Ours is a 330 g organic cotton, brushed lightly, and cut with a relaxed body so it sits over a tee without pulling.

We have worn the first sample twice a week for two winters. The cuffs have relaxed a little and the colour has softened from sage towards a greyer green, but the neck has not stretched and the hem still sits flat. It looks better than it did new.

If you wash it inside out in cool water and dry it flat or on low heat, it should do the same for you. That is the whole secret of a sweatshirt that lasts.

posts.title: A chore jacket that earns its pockets
posts.excerpt: Why the Chore Jacket has four pockets and a boxy cut, and what we changed after the first sample.
posts.content:
A chore jacket was once a work coat, and the good ones still are. Ours is a 10 oz cotton canvas in sage, with two chest pockets and two deep hand pockets that hold a phone, keys and a coffee cup without sagging.

The first sample was too stiff. We washed the canvas for longer, then softened the shoulders and shortened the sleeve by two centimetres. The final version feels worn in from the first day.

It is the one piece in the range that is meant to take a little punishment. Rain, bike handlebars, a bag strap. A few marks only make it look more like yours.

posts.title: How a parcel leaves the Portland studio
posts.excerpt: A look at how an order is folded, packed and sent, and why there is no plastic in the box.
posts.content:
Every order is packed at the same table where we cut patterns. A tee is folded in thirds, wrapped in a sheet of plain tissue and slid into a paper mailer made from recycled kraft paper. There is no plastic bag inside, no printed leaflet and no glossy card.

We write the order number by hand on the flap so we can find your parcel in the pile. The shipping label goes on last. Orders placed before noon Pacific leave the same day.

If something is wrong when it arrives, write to us. The person who packed your order will read your message.

posts.title: Washing linen: less than you think
posts.excerpt: Simple rules for washing and drying linen so it softens instead of wearing out.
posts.content:
Linen is one of the strongest natural fibres, and it gets stronger when wet. That is why a linen shirt can outlive almost everything else in your wardrobe, provided you do not treat it harshly.

Wash it cool, on a gentle cycle, with a mild detergent. Skip the fabric softener, which coats the fibres. Take it out of the machine while it is still damp and hang it to dry; do not tumble it hot.

Do not worry about creases. A linen shirt is meant to look lived in, and a quick shake before hanging is usually enough. If you do want to iron it, do it while it is still a little damp.

posts.title: The case for a little unevenness
posts.excerpt: Why the slub cotton in the Weekend Pocket Tee has small irregularities on purpose.
posts.content:
Slub cotton is spun with deliberate thick and thin patches in the yarn. The result is a fabric with a quiet texture, a dry hand and a surface that never looks flat or shiny.

We chose it for the Weekend Pocket Tee because it hides the small marks of a normal day. A fold from a bag strap or a stretch from a hanger does not show on a slightly uneven surface in the way it does on a smooth one.

It is also a little lighter than our everyday jersey, which makes it a good summer tee. It comes in sage, and a chest pocket holds whatever you need to hand.
